## About me

I am the Director of IT at R. Seelaus & Co., a broker-dealer and asset manager in Chatham, New Jersey, where I lead the firm's technology and work directly with the trading desks. In college I studied computer science and public policy, which sounds like an odd pair until you notice that most of finance is an incentive problem with a software problem sitting on top of it. My goal has stayed the same since then: to build solutions that make the financial markets work better for more of the people in them, not just the ones with the biggest technology budgets.

The analogy I keep coming back to is a full stack developer, except the stack is a trading floor. In a given week I might be building a pricing model, wiring an order router into the desk's workflow, standing up the cloud infrastructure underneath it and then sitting with a trader to figure out what the tool should actually do, which is usually not what anyone wrote down at the start.

## Career

**R. Seelaus & Co., Director of IT (March 2025 to present).** I run the firm's technology function and set its AI strategy. Specifically:

- I built an agentic research platform for institutional agency credit research. An LLM agent uses tools over proprietary and market data to answer a research question the way an analyst would, pulling the numbers first and writing second, and it is now part of how clients use the desk's research.
- I deployed LLM agents that automate the RFP (request for proposal) workflow across the broker-dealer and asset management businesses, cutting turnaround about 70%. For reference, a response that used to take a full week now takes about two days.
- I built an agency order routing and execution engine with round trips under 5 milliseconds, which grew the desk's agency order flow 50%. I also built a client analytics platform for the commercial paper desk, a systematic municipal bond market-making and pricing tool and real-time risk and capital monitoring for the desks and leadership.
- I moved the firm off an aging single-server setup onto serverless Google Cloud infrastructure, with the monitoring and CI/CD that every internal application now runs on. That includes the retrieval, evaluation and guardrail tooling that keeps the AI systems accurate and compliant, which in a regulated firm is not optional.

**Piper Sandler, Software Engineering Consultant (July 2021 to August 2024).** I worked with the municipal bond algorithmic trading desk, where I re-engineered the desk's production pricing engine in .NET. Better prices drove a 200% increase in quarterly trading turnover, meaning the desk tripled the business flowing through the engine. I also maintained the FIX protocol platform that monitors all external order flow across more than five counterparty connections, and built a deal pipeline tool that doubled new lead capture for the firm's top-ranked municipal finance team.

**Lynk Group, Founder (December 2020 to January 2025).** I founded Lynk to apply quantitative methods to pari-mutuel wagering and led a team of five. We built the data pipelines and models, a low-latency C#/.NET wagering system that ran at 99.9% uptime for more than a year, which works out to less than nine hours of downtime in twelve months, and an LLM that let users query a decade of racing data in plain English.

**Education.** University of Denver, B.A. in Computer Science with Distinction and Public Policy (2021), University Honors Program.

**Outside of work.** I spent a semester with NOLS on an 80-day, 500-mile expedition in Baja, Mexico, backpacking, sea kayaking and sailing, and my peers picked me to lead a five-day kayaking expedition around Isla San Jose. Nobody got lost, which I still count as my best leadership result. These days it is skiing, cooking and music whenever I can.

## Passion project: quantitative wagering

Lynk started as a company and is now the project I keep coming back to. I think horse racing is one of the best laboratories there is for quantitative finance, because every price is public, every result is final and the fees are posted on the wall. The market is pari-mutuel, meaning everyone bets against each other in a shared pool and the track keeps a cut off the top before paying out the rest. That cut, called the takeout, runs about 15 to 30 cents of every dollar depending on the bet, which is a far bigger toll than any stock exchange charges, and it falls hardest on the casual bettors who have no edge to cover it. Therefore the questions are the same ones I care about in markets generally: is the crowd's price efficient, where is it wrong, who pays for the mistakes and how much can you bet before your own money moves the price against you?

The research below covers 648,670 races from 2012 to 2025, which is roughly 130 races a day, every day, for fourteen years. Each paper follows the same outline I use for every project: the problem, the data, the approach, the results, what the work does not do yet and where it goes next.

::: {.card-grid}

::: {.card}
### [Handicapping Without the Tote](reports/fundamental-model.qmd)
What actually predicts a horse race when you are not allowed to look at the betting odds: feature families, walk-forward results from 2019 to 2025, a neural network that reads the whole field and online ratings for trainers, jockeys and sires.
:::

::: {.card}
### [One Race, One Winner](reports/multiclass.qmd)
Why framing the problem as "which horse in this race wins" instead of "does this horse win" was one of the most valuable decisions in the whole project, tested head to head on the same data.
:::

::: {.card}
### [Sizing the Bet](reports/bet-sizing.qmd)
From the one-line Kelly formula to a nonlinear solver that sizes bets across win, place, show and exacta pools while accounting for how my own money moves the price.
:::

::: {.card}
### [Lynk: the code](code/lynk-framework.qmd)
The open-source Python framework that came out of this research: probabilities, Kelly sizing, pari-mutuel math, leakage-safe backtesting and a horse racing module, built so new markets can plug into the same core.
:::

:::

**A note on scope:** these papers describe the methods and the fundamental (no odds) model in full. However, the proprietary models, the specific betting strategies and their returns are intentionally left out.
